articles.title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
articles.summary:
Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum

In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl…

blocks.text: In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions.

They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets.

Also on display are protective ritual objects, taken by the British from Gaidinliu’s hiding places, which they believed she had used against them. These are a stick with a monkey skull used to ward off evil spirits, and small wooden clubs, traditionally used by Naga people to cast an omen on an enemy.

The exhibition, The Afterlives of Captured Objects, raises questions about the colonial extraction of artefacts from Indigenous communities, which were often originally catalogued using prejudiced and discriminatory language, according to the curator, Clare Harris, a professor of visual anthropology.

For example, Harris said Gaidinliu’s notebooks were derided as “meaningless scribbling” by the colonial anthropologist JP Mills, who collected them. But he also recorded that these writings “gave her immense prestige”, which suggests that they may have been seized as part of British efforts to suppress the religious and political movement that Gaidinliu led, called Heraka.

blocks.caption: Rani Gaidinliu has long been revered as an important leader in the resistance movement that led to Indian independence. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

blocks.text: While most of the objects on display were taken by the British after Gaidinliu abandoned them while on the run, two items were more violently extracted. Textiles displayed on mannequins in the show were taken from a pair of male and female sacred clay figures from a Heraka temple in the village of Kambiron in 1931.
The textiles are shown along with a photograph taken by a British officer of another soldier kneeling with the sacred figures, which were destroyed along with the temple.

“By showing the photograph at the same time, you can make the equation visually about what was extracted by the British there,” said Harris. “The British destroy the temple and they destroy the figures, so they take away the potency of those things.”

blocks.caption: Naga women photographing copies of Gaidinliu’s notebooks. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

blocks.text: The show follows a four-year project by researchers from India and the Universities of Edinburgh and Oxford to digitise the Gaidinliu collection and share it with Naga communities in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. Their craftspeople have used the images to revive and revitalise traditional crafts such as basket weaving and textile making, with some of their creations included in the exhibition.

Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at the school of divinity, University of Edinburgh, who co-led the project with Harris, said attempts were also being made to translate Gaidinliu’s notebooks in an effort to reconstruct a new Indigenous language for the Naga people.
He said: “There are some symbols which are recognisable within stories and myths. They may be untranslatable in a conventional sense but they are being used to try and construct a language system.”
after newsletter promotion

The exhibition also aims to raise international recognition of Gaidinliu, who has long been revered as an important leader in the resistance movement that led to Indian independence. After her release from prison in 1947, she became head of a political movement advocating for recognition of a Naga homeland.

blocks.caption: Gaidinliu was imprisoned in 1932 at the age of 17. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

blocks.text: Alila Chang, one of Gaidinliu’s grandnieces, said her family felt a deep sense of pride about the exhibition. She said: “These objects are connected to our family’s history and the struggles and sacrifices of our people as well. We want the world to know her struggles and for what reason she fought.”
Chang, who has come to Oxford for the exhibition’s private view, also shared a more personal recollection of Gaidinliu as a “very affectionate grandmother”.
“I remember [her] giving us sweets,” she said, adding how Gaidinliu, who died in 1993, would pray for her and her sibling when they went to school in the morning.
“She will always be in our hearts, but I think she belongs to the world now.”

articles.title: Israeli strikes kill 16 schoolchildren so far this month, Gaza ministry says
articles.summary:
Statement follows death of sisters, aged 15 and 13, in airstrike on residential apartment in Gaza City

Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of…
articles.byline: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as young people across the territory face intensifying bombardment and struggle to find food, clean water and shelter.

On Wednesday, Gaza’s ministry of education said: “Palestinian students had been targeted for the third time in less than 24 hours, in an escalation reflecting the continued Israeli violations against children in the Gaza Strip.”
“The number of schoolchildren killed since the beginning of November has now risen to 16,” it added.
The statement follows the death of two sisters, Yusra, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 13, in the early hours of Wednesday in an airstrike targeting a residential apartment in western Gaza City.
Yusra was a pupil at Kafr Qasim school, while her sister Jana attended al-Manar private school.

The ministry added: “The girls’ father, Mohammed Majed Abu Al-Ouf, and their mother, Noura Ezzat Abu Al-Ouf, were also killed in the strike which injured several other Palestinians.” The father was a director of internal security services for Hamas in northern Gaza.
Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

blocks.caption: Palestinian children outside a residential block hit by Israeli strikes in Gaza City in 2025. Photograph: Ebrahim Hajjaj/Reuters

blocks.text: On 6 November, Mohammed Nidal Barbakh, 15, was shot by Israeli forces in the Bir 19 area of al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, and later died from his injuries.
He was in the 10th grade at the Muscat school and dreamed of becoming a professional football player.

“That day, after lunch, Mohammed went to the sports academy at 1.30pm to take part in training,” his father, Dr Nidal Mohammed Barbakh, said. “An Israeli tank had advanced and positioned itself on a nearby hill before firing two rounds towards the pitch. One of them ricocheted after hitting a metal object, striking Mohammed in the back and exiting through his neck.

“He was talented and an excellent student. He was killed at the age of 15, on a sports pitch in al-Mawasi, an area where people had been told to go because it was considered safe. I do not absolve the Israeli army of responsibility for what happened. It kills every ambition within us and buries our children’s dreams before they have a chance to come true.”
On 13 November, Israeli artillery shelling killed three people in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, including a father and his 12-year-old son, Ahmed Abu Daher, as well as a woman.

blocks.caption: Palestinians transport the body of Ahmed Abu Daher, 12, outside al-Aqsa hospital in central Gaza Strip. Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP

blocks.text: Ahmed dreamed of becoming an Arabic language teacher, like his grandfather Saleh, said his mother, Walaa Abu Daher.

“That day, my husband was heading to a condolence gathering in the al-Qastal area, east of Deir al-Balah,” Daher said. “Ahmed asked his father if he could accompany him. While they were at the gathering, they were targeted by Israeli artillery fire. Ahmed ran to ask the people attending the gathering for help. He then rushed back towards his father when a second shell was fired. Shrapnel struck Ahmed in his legs, abdomen and head.
“I cannot describe how deeply their loss has affected me. I feel as though my life stopped that day,” she added.
The Israel Defense Forces have been approached for comment.
Thousands of school-age children and hundreds of education workers have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza, while tens of thousands of children have been unable to attend school regularly.

On Thursday, Israeli attacks killed at least nine Palestinians across Gaza, including Khaled Abu Nada, the undersecretary of Gaza’s ministry of education, and his wife, according to health officials, as attacks continued despite the ceasefire in the territory.
A few days ago, the ministry of education said Israel’s attacks against students, civilian leaders and teachers were “part of a systematic assault on the Palestinian education system”.
According to Unicef, 98% of school buildings in Gaza have sustained damage, with more than 93% requiring major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, while approximately 81% were directly hit.

blocks.caption: Displaced Palestinians shelter in a destroyed school building in Khan Younis in 2024. Photograph: Hatem Khaled/Reuters

blocks.text: Young Palestinians in Gaza face a fourth winter in overcrowded tents and makeshift shelters, with limited access to basic services as the humanitarian and public health crisis deepens.

Children and young people are among those most vulnerable to meningitis, for which Gaza’s health ministry issued an epidemic alert on Tuesday after a sharp rise in infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid.

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza over the last three years, according to the territory’s health ministry. More than 20,000 children have been reported killed by Israeli strikes.

articles.title: Politician hosts 400,000 guests at daughter’s wedding in India’s poorest state
articles.summary:
Six helipads built and feast prepared by 500 cooks for wedding hosted by Anant Singh, an MP charged with murder

It takes a brave soul to try to match

blocks.text: It takes a brave soul to try to match the mythic opulence of the wedding arranged by the Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani for his son Anant in 2024. Estimates of the cost for the months-long celebration ran to at least $600m, with world leaders and celebrities among those on the guest list.

Smaller fry though he is, Anant Singh, a legislator in India’s poorest state, Bihar, gave it his best shot on Wednesday, albeit in a rustic rural setting, for the nuptials of his daughter Shivangi Singh, and Rishikesh Kumar, an MBA student from Georgia State University in Atlanta.

blocks.caption: Shivangi Singh (left) and Rishikesh Kumar during their wedding.  Photograph: NDTV

blocks.text: About 400,000 guests were hosted across 2.5 hectares at the family home in the village of Nadawa – a staggering figure even by the standards of India’s famed extravagant weddings. Guests were treated to 500,000 pieces of traditional sweets, and a feast prepared by an army of 500 chefs and cooks, Singh’s confidant Munna Singh told Agence France-Presse. One thousand kilos of mutton were reportedly used for kebabs and curries. Six makeshift helipads were erected for VIPs flying in from across India.
Kumar arrived at the venue in sunglasses and waving an orange scarf in a convoy of 151 cars (Hindus consider uneven numbers to be lucky). Among the gifts for the groom was a Land Rover Defender.

The roads leading to the venue were so choked with cars before the wedding that one guest escaped the gridlock, The Times of India reported, by jumping on a tractor and driving across the surrounding fields.
Guests were also treated to elaborate flower arrangements featuring blooms imported from China and a fireworks display.

Instead of a DJ for entertainment, Singh planned a horse race. Gatecrashers clambered up into trees and on to electricity towers to catch a glimpse of the race, but the chaos and tumult was so great it had to be cancelled at the 11th hour. Lying around somewhere amid the wedding detritus was the SUV that would have gone to the winner.

blocks.caption: A screengrab showing crowds at the wedding. Photograph: NDTV

blocks.text: Singh is a controversial figure. Elected five times to the state assembly, he has 28 criminal cases pending against him ranging from murder and attempted murder to extortion and kidnapping. All the cases are listed on the website of the Association for Democratic Reforms, an NGO that is trying to improve governance and strengthen democracy. Singh denies any wrongdoing regarding the charges.

In a television interview before the wedding, he pooh poohed the idea that there was anything unusual about the scale of the wedding preparations. “I laid on exactly the same thing for my elder daughter,” he said.
India’s wedding season has just kicked off. Between now and 15 December, an estimated 5.2m weddings are expected to take place across the country.

articles.title: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
articles.summary:
The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid?

Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present…

blocks.text: Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.
It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

blocks.caption: Lana Nusseibeh in March, when she was the UAE’s minister of state. Photograph: Abdelhadi Ramahi/Reuters

blocks.text: Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK, all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.
The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.
“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the ​military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE, have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.
The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.
A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

blocks.caption: Fighters who defected from the RSF gathered in western Omdurman, Sudan, earlier this month. Photograph: Marwan Ali/AP

blocks.text: Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”
That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.
Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

articles.title: Israel ‘officially sanctions’ torture of Palestinian prisoners to extract confessions, report concludes
articles.summary:
Public Committee Against Torture in Israel examined 42 complaints against Shin Bet interrogators over past decade

Israel has institutionalised the use of torture to extract confessions from…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison and Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Israel has institutionalised the use of torture to extract confessions from Palestinian prisoners, sometimes documenting abuse in official records or granting advanced approval for “special measures” in interrogation, according to a report from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI).
This dangerous practice risked leading to irreversible miscarriages of justice, as Israel moved to implement a racist new death penalty law that targets Palestinians, the report said.
PCATI examined 42 cases in which Palestinians filed complaints about the use of torture by Shin Bet interrogators over the last decade.
More than three-quarters said they confessed after the use of “torture or other illegal methods”, and one in 10 provided incriminating statements about other people under torture.

“When it comes to Palestinian detainees, the Israeli legal system officially sanctions torture as a tool for extracting confessions, regardless of whether the content of those confessions is true,” said Sari Bashi, the executive director of PCATI.
“Torture as a tool of interrogation is particularly egregious given initiatives to impose the death penalty in Israel for the first time since 1962.”

Over the years, in hundreds of testimonies, Palestinian detainees have consistently described interrogations employing extreme sleep deprivation, physical violence such as slapping and kicking, threats, sexual violence and being held in stress positions.

Some of this abuse is also laid out in the official records of Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security service. PCATI details the case of a Palestinian lawyer arrested in February 2019 who was subjected to extreme sleep deprivation.

During an interrogation period lasting 27.5 days, or 660 hours, he was questioned for more than 552 hours, an average of 20 hours a day, with one session lasting nearly 48 hours. Some of the remaining 108 hours were spent travelling to and attending detention hearings.

In a 1999 ruling, Israel’s supreme court explicitly prohibited sleep deprivation as a deliberate interrogation method. Despite this, the lawyer was convicted of involvement in shooting attacks based on information extracted during this period.
The state inspector for complaints about Shin Bet interrogations (Mavtan) ruled that the interrogations took place in accordance with procedures, PCATI said.
More than 1,680 torture complaints were filed between 2001 and 2024 with Mavtan. None have led to an indictment.
Other cases are indirectly documented in Israeli judicial records, although judges rarely accept testimony about torture of Palestinians, PCATI said.

In one case, a detainee’s false confession, made under torture, was used as evidence by prosecutors. The man was released after his lawyer presented proof that he was not present at the scene of the crime, PCATI said.
Sleep deprivation was the most frequently used form of torture in complaints examined by PCATI, but more than half included the use of stress positions and other forms of physical violence.

Israel is a signatory to the UN convention against torture, but its legal system has effectively codified the use of violence and abuse where it is deemed “necessary” to extract life-saving information, PCATI said.

In a “necessity interrogation” or “military interrogation”, Shin Bet officials torture detainees “after consulting with their superiors and following an internal procedure for documenting their decisions and conduct”, the report said.

“[A] supposedly narrow exception ballooned and developed into a sprawling system of legal and administrative exceptions that swallowed the so-called rule, enabling the use of violence while maintaining the appearance of prohibition,” it continued.

There is no publicly available information on the scale of “necessity interrogations” inside the Shin Bet, PCATI said. They are an urgent concern as Israel moves to end a de facto moratorium on the death penalty, which had stood since the 1962 execution of the Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann.

“The death penalty is always wrong, because it’s cruel, irreversible and negates the right to life. No one should be executed, particularly not in a system tainted by systematic violence,” Bashi said.
In March, the Knesset passed a racist law allowing the execution of Palestinians convicted of terror charges over deadly attacks, but not Jewish Israelis who commit similar crimes.
In the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians are tried in military courts, execution is now the default punishment for a defendant found guilty of deadly terror attacks.
The legislation drew fierce international criticism, including from the UN’s high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, who warned that it would constitute a war crime if enacted.
A separate law empowers a special tribunal to impose death sentences in cases arising from the 7 October 2023 attacks.
Even in rare cases where courts have excluded confessions obtained under torture, Israeli case law allows prosecutors to use information derived from them as evidence to secure convictions.

PCATI said that as detention conditions worsened after October 2023, rights groups documented a sharp rise in violence by Israeli prison guards and soldiers, including beatings, attacks with dogs, electric shocks, threats and rape.

At least 103 Palestinian detainees have died in Israeli custody since 7 October 2023. Of 10 postmortems reviewed by Physicians for Human Rights Israel, five showed signs of physical assault and six showed evidence of medical neglect.
The Israel Prison Service said “all prisoners are held in accordance with the law”. The Shin Bet and Israel’s justice ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: ‘Trapped in grief’: wife of Japanese journalist detained by Russia pleads for his release
articles.summary:
Yuki Imai being held in Moscow on allegations he conducted ‘espionage’ while working for a newspaper in Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east

The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been…

blocks.text: The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying has issued an emotive appeal for his release.

Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid-October as he was preparing to return to Japan from a two-year assignment at the Japanese newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east.

Russian authorities alleged that Imai had been “conducting espionage activities” on the island, collecting information about Russian defence capabilities he intended to pass on to Japanese intelligence. Both the newspaper and Japan’s prime minster, Sanae Takaichi, have denied the claims.

His detention has inflamed tensions between Tokyo and Moscow and prompted Takaichi to request Imai’s release during a meeting with the Russian leader Vladimir Putin at last week’s Apec summit in China.

The arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over islands in the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido – which Russia has administered since the dying days of the second world war.
In a statement released to media organisations through the Hokkaido Shimbun, Imai’s wife, Nozomi Imai, said her husband’s plight meant his family were “trapped in grief”.

“Since his detention, his parents and I have spent every day worrying about him” she said in the statement, published in Japanese, English and Russian. Recalling the moment she saw TV footage of her husband being taken away by Russian authorities, she said: “I could hardly breathe. It felt as if my heart were being ripped apart.”

She added: “No one could remain calm after seeing a beloved family member with his arms bound behind his back. In the video, I could even see the souvenirs in his suitcase – the gifts he was bringing home for us. I could not sleep even for a moment that night. When morning came, it still did not feel real. I could not even cry.”

Imai, 34, has barely seen his infant daughter, who was born during his posting to Russia. “He had been so looking forward to coming home,” Nozomi Imai wrote. “During his posting, our daughter was born. She is now 21 months old, and he loves her more than words can say. He had even said excitedly that he wanted to be the one to pick her up from daycare on the very day he got home.”

blocks.caption: Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east. Photograph: Gribov Andrei/Alamy

blocks.text: Japanese diplomats have been permitted to visit Imai only twice since he was detained, although he has had several meetings with lawyers appointed by his employer.

Japan’s ambassador to Moscow, Akira Muto, said he had met the journalist at Lefortovo detention centre in Moscow this week and that he appeared to be in good health. Japanese embassy officials were also granted access to Imai at the end of October.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai had been engaged in “ordinary news gathering” on Sakhalin, adding the newspaper did “not conduct reporting or gather information based on government directions”.

Shortly after his arrest, Takaichi denied Imai had been spying. “There is no such fact,” she told reporters, adding that “the protection of Japanese nationals is extremely important right now, and we intend to focus our efforts on that.”
Concerns are growing that Moscow will seek to make an example of Imai in protest at Japan’s support for sanctions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Russia’s Federal Security Service, which is investigating Imai, has not commented publicly since it announced the reporter’s arrest. His detention is scheduled to expire on 12 December but could be extended, the Kyodo news agency said.

The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai, whose grandfather was born on Sakhalin, was an admirer of Russian culture who had used his position to promote grassroots exchanges.He even hosted Russian visitors at his home in the Hokkaido city of Nemuro.
Nozomi Imai, who said she and her husband had met as students through their shared love of Russian films and novels, said his detention was taking a toll on his ageing parents.

“They worry whether they will ever see their beloved only son again in their lifetime,” she wrote. “Yuki Imai is not only a journalist. He is a beloved son, husband, and father. Please – please return this precious papa to his little daughter.”

articles.title: Watch: BBC confronts German man suspected of supplying migrant gangs with small boats
articles.summary: Marvin Reuter is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

blocks.text: A German boat dealer is suspected of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings to the UK, in the first four months of 2026, allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.
His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.
We confronted the 35-year-old at his business, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

articles.title: Trump tariff threat ‘unacceptable’, says Brazil, as China denounces levies as baseless
articles.summary: Brazil indignant about proposed tariffs on sugar and aircraft, while Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’

blocks.text: Brazil has said it will not bend to the new US tariff “threat” and China accused Washington of “political manipulation” in the wake of Donald Trump’s latest economic salvo against 14 major trading partners.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday: “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.
It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

Brazil was particularly singled out for in the announcement after trade talks stalled. The Trump administration claimed on Wednesday that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries.

The new tariffs are being imposed under a law which allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”
The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. The US said China would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%. The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”
Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”
Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.
It added it was “preparing ​and submitting ​rebuttal comments on the ​preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions ​and allegations ‌made by ​interested ​parties.”

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.
Taiwan was also singled out for new tariffs, but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech product which account for ​over 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.
Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, and Thailand.
Tokyo’s top government spokesman, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.
However Democratic Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”

“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs,” Wyden added. “Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”
With Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: Palestinian journalist killed by Israel in Gaza wins Rory Peck prize
articles.summary:
Mariam Dagga shares award with two of her colleagues from AP for ‘powerful coverage’ of human cost of war

Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in…

blocks.text: Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza in an Israeli strike, has posthumously won the prestigious Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists, the organisers announced on Wednesday.

She shares the award with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press (AP), Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi, “for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war” in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said.
Dagga, who has a teenage son named Ghaith, was killed in August 2025 in an Israeli airstrike on a southern Gaza hospital, which claimed the lives of four other journalists.
The independent photographer and reporter had been working with the AP news agency since the beginning of the current conflict, triggered by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.

Dagga was renowned for her relentless reporting despite the personal losses she suffered throughout the war. She filmed the death of a protester who was shot during the 2018 Great March of Return in Gaza, when Israeli forces shot protesters marching towards the Gaza border fence, killing more than 220 people and wounding more than 9,200. She later discovered that the protester was her brother.
The war correspondent continued her work as a journalist during the war in Gaza over the last 22 months, working as a freelancer with the AP and Independent Arabia.

blocks.caption: Mariam Dagga’s father holds a camera and mobile phone belonging to his daughter after she was killed in August 2025. Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP

blocks.text: The AP’s executive editor, Julie Pace, said: “Journalists play an essential role in documenting events and informing the public, often at enormous personal risk.
“We honour Mariam and all journalists killed during this conflict and other conflicts – and remain committed to seeking answers about their deaths.”
French photographer Robin Tutenges was the recipient of the first Rory Peck award for photojournalism in recognition of his work on the conflict in Ethiopia’s northern Amhara region.

Sudanese freelance photographer and video journalist Ahmed Mohamed Abdalla, who works with Agence France-Presse, was shortlisted for the same award for his coverage of the fall of El Fasher to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Sudan’s civil war.
Abdalla was not allowed to attend the prize-giving ceremony in London as the UK government refused to grant him a visa.

In a recorded video message shared during the ceremony, he told of how the capital of the North Darfur region’s besieged inhabitants had to eat livestock feed to survive amid the daily deluge of missiles.
The prize has been awarded since 1995 in memory of Northern Irish video journalist Rory Peck, who was killed in Moscow in 1993, to celebrate the work of freelance video journalists.

articles.title: At least 30 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
articles.summary:
Blaze on ring road surrounding Egyptian capital injures at least 25 people and leaves cars and motorcycles charred

A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway…

blocks.text: A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 30 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 25 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, the public prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
The stretch of the highway where the crash occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, according to the health ministry.

blocks.caption: Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb, where charred vehicles remained after the blaze. Photograph: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/Reuters

blocks.text: At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.
The Egyptian president, Abdel-Fattah al-Sissi, expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The public prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were under way to identify the victims.

The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further.

Deadly traffic incidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.
In January, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

articles.title: Lululemon founder stuns Canadian women’s leadership conference with sexist comments
articles.summary:
Chip Wilson said men importing brides from Thailand was due to women waiting too long to have children

The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in

blocks.text: The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in Canada are having too few children and this could lead some men to bring in brides from Thailand, in remarks that stunned audience members at a women’s leadership conference.

Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. The organization says it aims to create space for “candid conversations about the barriers women face both in business and society”.

Wilson’s talk on 23 November, titled “Little Black Stretchy Pants” after his memoir, was billed as an “intimate, fireside chat” offering insight into the “mind and instincts of the man himself”. It was moderated by Nuvyn Peters, CEO of Axis Connects.

There is no publicly available video of the event, but the Guardian spoke with people who attended it and reviewed social media posts from those present. Outrage over the event was first reported by the Globe and Mail.

According to people who were there, Wilson told the audience that companies would be reluctant to hire a 22-year-old woman because she might become pregnant at 23 and take maternity leave. He went on to suggest that women were waiting too long to have children, prompting men to import brides from Thailand.
“There were audible gasps in the room and everyone was clearly uncomfortable. It was a mix of disengaging, walking out and also just complete shock of what was being said on stage,” one person said.

“I am floored that Axis gave this man a platform. We all were saying before the event it was surprising he was there – and it’s clear that [Wilson] runs in the organizer’s circles after she opened with the fact that they go on walks [at a Vancouver mountain] together.”
The event, which was supposed to run for an hour, was cut short at 45 minutes.

The remarks are not the first time Wilson has attracted criticism for his comments about women and their bodies. He stepped down as chair of Lululemon’s board in 2013 after the company’s signature black yoga pants were criticized for being see-through and Wilson blamed the problem on the body types of some customers.
On Monday, he reportedly told the group that those prior comments about body types had been “misconstrued” and said he was referring to women who wear sizes that are too small.
Wilson, who is believed to be worth more than C$6bn, has not had a leadership role at Lululemon for several years but remains a major shareholder.
He also reportedly told the audience that poverty had largely been eradicated, and that he was looking forward to going to space with Elon Musk.

Audience members also said Wilson suggested that men were better suited to helm clothing companies that catered to women, because they knew what looked good on women’s bodies. He said the same was true of women who lead companies focused on men’s fashion.

“We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the Leadership Forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects,” Peters said in a statement. “We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community. His comments also underscore an uncomfortable reality: attitudes and assumptions that hold women back in the workplace and in leadership have not disappeared. Challenging those attitudes is central to the work and ethos of Axis Connects.”

Wilson’s spokesperson pointed to the work the Lululemon founder has done to mentor and “empower” women in leadership roles over the years and said his efforts “speak for themselves”. A number of women who were early employees of the company and worked closely with Wilson became millionaires when the company went public, he has previously noted in his memoir, and have gone on to found their own businesses.

More than 700 women attended the conference, many representing organizations they worked for. One person said the experience left her “irate”, adding that it was also indicative of what women continued to tolerate.
“It’s just sad that this is what women still have to deal with, in a forum literally for women.”

articles.title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
articles.summary:
Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged

A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of…

blocks.text: A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

The nine workers had their contracts terminated in January 2024 “in the interests of the agency” and were told in termination letters that the allegations against them were “very serious and credible”. The dismissals were confirmed after a UN investigation found they might have been involved in the 7 October attacks.

The decision, which was taken by former Unrwa commissioner general Philippe Lazzarini after consultation with the UN secretary general, António Guterres, was apparently made in the hope that appeasing Israel and its allies would allow humanitarian work to continue in Gaza.

blocks.caption: Philippe Lazzarini, a former UN aid chief, took the decision to dismiss the nine Palestinian staff. Photograph: Heiko Junge/Reuters

blocks.text: Critics warned at the time that the decision, on the basis of allegations rather than evidence, compromised the UN’s integrity and had the opposite effect, giving credence to unproven allegations.
The dismissals failed to prevent the Biden administration ordering a pause in funding, a measure that was echoed temporarily by other backers, leading to a financial shortfall of $450m (£340m).

“I have always said on the record that the Israeli allegations against Unrwa were the mother of all lies,” said Chris Gunness, a former Unrwa spokesperson “Sacking the workers without any evidence confirmed their guilt unfairly in the minds of journalists, led 16 top donors to abandon Unrwa and produced the worst financial crisis in the agency’s history, from which it may never recover.”
The Unrwa dispute tribunal that ruled in favour of one of its sacked workers, Abu Awad, described the Israeli allegations as unsupported and of “limited evidentiary value and reliability”.

The tribunal also found that an internal UN investigation had not interviewed the 19 staff members initially accused by Israel of involvement in the 7 October attacks because of “safety and security” concerns.
“The allegations against the applicant and the other staff members, it seems, are therefore based almost entirely on information in Israel’s possession,” the tribunal said.

It cast doubt on intercepted mobile phone conversations and messages offered by Israel as evidence, noting that one case had involved mistaken identity based on a cloned sim card, a common phenomenon in Gaza.

It also said that voice recognition claims made by Israel were dubious and some transcripts of conversations were found by UN investigators not to support claims that they proved links to Hamas or the 7 October attacks.

The allegation against Awad was that he was a “platoon commander” in Hamas’s military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, a claim he rejected. He was not alleged to have physically taken part in the 7 October attack and witness statements to the tribunal said he was on an Unrwa staff bus as normal.

blocks.caption: Israeli soldiers on patrol by the Unrwa headquarters in Gaza City in 2024. Many countries paused funding for the UN agency after Israel made allegations against some of its Palestinian staff. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters

blocks.text: The specific allegation against Awad was that he “had been instructed in a telephone call intercepted by Israeli intelligence to monitor the events of 7 October 2023, while simultaneously receiving Hamas intelligence updates related to the attacks”.
The tribunal said the Israeli security services had failed to clarify who was alleged to have made the call to Awad and in what way the mobile phone that received the call was associated with him.

Unrwa did not respond to a request for comment. Asked by the tribunal to provide evidence underpinning the dismissal of the workers, the agency cited the Israeli government as well as a report in the Times of Israel and another on the website UN Watch, a pro-Israel pressure group that has campaigned against Unrwa.

In its ruling, the tribunal said Unrwa’s claim that the cited sources had informed the decision to dismiss the workers was “open to some doubt” because all the supporting documents it had submitted were produced after the disputed decision was made on 26 January 2024.

Lazzarini, a Swiss humanitarian expert who left the commissioner general post in March, did not respond to a request for comment. In February 2024, he admitted his decision to sack the workers represented “reverse due process” in that the investigation followed the dismissal.

“My judgment, based on this going public, true or untrue, was I need to take the swiftest and boldest decision to show that as an agency we take this allegation seriously,” he said, adding that “the ability of the entire agency to continue to operate and deliver critical humanitarian assistance was at stake”.

The tribunal said it could not decide on the allegations against Awad but ruled that Unrwa had failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to sack him. It awarded him a year’s pay and $5,000 for “moral damages”.

In the wake of its allegations against the sacked workers, Israel claimed that Unrwa was heavily infiltrated by Hamas and its parliament voted in 2024 to ban the agency from operating in Israel or in the occupied Palestinian territories.

The international court of justice stated in October 2025, however, that “Israel has not substantiated its allegations that a significant part of Unrwa’s employees are members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions”.

articles.title: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations
articles.summary:
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station

China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space…

blocks.text: China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

Tiangong, completed in 2022, is the jewel in the crown of China’s space programme. The government has invested billions into its celestial ambitions in recent years to catch up with the US and Russia, two of the five partners involved in the ISS, along with Europe, Japan and Canada. After 25 years of continuous occupation, the ISS is set to cease operations from 2030, according to Nasa.
On Wednesday China’s president, Xi Jinping, told his Pakistani counterpart Beijing was “willing to work with all countries … to uphold the banner of the peaceful use of outer space”.
Ali was part of the crew of Shenzhou 24, the most recent iteration of the series of missions that rotate astronauts in the space station every six months. He is the first Pakistani to reach orbit.

blocks.caption: People watching a broadcast of China’s Shenzhou 24 mission in Islamabad, Pakistan. Photograph: Sohail Shahzad/EPA

blocks.text: “Sending another country’s astronaut to space is a major undertaking,” Blaine Curcio, the managing director at Orbital Gateway Consulting, told the Guardian. “Pakistan is putting a lot of trust into Beijing by having him fly into space on a Chinese-built rocket. There are also considerations related to security: Ali is getting detailed insights into China’s crewed space programme … It makes China better prepared to do it again, and also makes it clear to other countries that China is open to this type of collaboration.”

Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s. China has launched Pakistani satellites and a Pakistani-built rover ‌is also due to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.

Shenzhou 24 blasted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China against a pink-tinged dawn sky on Wednesday, footage showed, and first docked with the space station three and a half hours later.

Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, will conduct experiments including one cultivating microalgae as a potential food and another testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds. To prepare for the mission, he ​trained for seven months in Beijing, including intensive Chinese-language classes.

At a press conference the day before the launch, Ali recited a line from a classical Chinese poem. Commander Tang Hongbo told reporters that differences in language and culture had made learning to work together more challenging, but that the effort had paid off.

Ali will not stay for the six-month term usually demanded of Tiangong astronauts. Instead, he will return to earth with two of the Shenzhou 23 crew while its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain to complete another milestone – the first full-year stay in space by a Chinese astronout.

Beijing’s accelerated achievements in the skies have spooked its rivals. China is the third country to put humans in orbit and has landed robotic rovers on Mars and the moon, where it hopes to send crewed missions within the next decade. In racing to the moon before 2030, Beijing is competing with the US’s Artemis programme. The US has excluded China from the ISS since 2011, banning Nasa from collaborating with Beijing. In 2025 Nasa went further by blocking Chinese citizens from its facilities altogether.

“We know that China is quite keen to develop Tiangong as an international hub,” said Curcio, pointing to China Manned Space Agency documents published in coordination with the UN outlining “resources for international cooperation” onboard the station.

In the future, he said, he would expect countries such as Brazil and Egypt to seek out the opportunity to send astronauts on Chinese missions. He added: “I think when the ISS is retired, if there is no western replacement (government or commercial), then yes, we may eventually see European or other ISS-involved countries – like Russia – send astronauts to Tiangong.”

articles.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
articles.summary:
Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park

A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists…

blocks.text: A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.
“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

blocks.caption: An African forest elephant. Photograph: Danita Delimont/Alamy

blocks.text: Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media.

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.
Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.
after newsletter promotion

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund.

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation, which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.
A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

articles.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
articles.summary:
Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections

The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual…

blocks.text: The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.

Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC. He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.

A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.

The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”

She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.

Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].”

A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”
Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.

Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”
after newsletter promotion

She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.
Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.

Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

articles.title: Indian Cockroach movement leader asks court for permission to fly to UK
articles.summary:
Officials at Delhi airport stopped Saurav Das from boarding flight to Britain, where students have invited him to speak

A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi…

blocks.text: A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi high court to give him permission to fly to the UK after immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him boarding a flight early on Tuesday morning.

The court is scheduled to hear Saurav Das’s case on Thursday morning. His lawyer asked the court for a quick hearing because Das has by now already missed some of his engagements at British universities and can only attend the other events on his itinerary if he is allowed to fly out as soon as possible.
Das, 27, is one of the main faces of the Cockroach movement, which shot into the political firmament out of nowhere in May to challenge the Narendra Modi government with street protests.
The movement succeeded in forcing the education minister to resign in July over exam leaks and has since functioned as a pressure group.
Das had been invited by the Oxford Union Society to participate in a “fireside chat” on the movement.
Indian student groups at Edinburgh, Cambridge, Queen Mary University of London and the London School of Economics have also invited him to speak.
“Students want to know how we succeeded without any violence, how we began and where we are going. There is a great curiosity about the movement,” Das told the Guardian.
Reports in the Indian media have alleged that Das was informed well before the flight that his passport contained discrepancies.

“None of these reports is true,” said Das. “I received an email five hours before my flight saying that I should not use my passport for travel. It gave no reason. And I did not see the email until I arrived at Delhi airport. What’s more, I’ve travelled abroad before on this passport since it was issued in 2019 so what’s the problem with it now?”

He suspects that the government is using a frivolous case filed in Chennai against him as a pretext. The case has been filed, Das surmises, by someone hostile to the Cockroach movement and disputes his citizenship.

Das believes he was deliberately stopped by a government that is “scared” of someone such as him speaking abroad about the ideals of Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru (independent India’s first prime minister) and that it wanted to make an example of him.
“It’s a chilling signal to young Indians that we can do what we like, that if we can do this to a leader of a movement, we can do this to you too,” said Das.
after newsletter promotion
In recent years, the government has stopped foreign speakers and academics, including several from the UK, from entering India.

Last year, Francesca Orsini, a professor at Soas University of London, was stopped at Delhi airport and deported despite holding a valid visa. The government said she had been blacklisted for allegedly conducting research and speaking at events while visiting on a tourist visa in 2024.
Also last year, Nitasha Kaul, a professor at Westminster University, was detained at Bangalore airport and deported for “anti-India activities”.

Some people who find themselves blacklisted have chosen to fight back. In 2023, the UK-based journalist Amrit Wilson had her overseas citizen of India card which allows free movement into India cancelled, also for alleged “anti-India activities”.
She took legal action and earlier this week, the Delhi high court ruled that the government had failed to give any concrete details of what it meant by “anti-India activities”.
The court has given the government a week to issue a fresh notice, this time giving specific reasons.

articles.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, says president
articles.summary:
Operation in which one hostage-taker was killed ends daylong siege in Cartegena shopping centre, where 30 people were initially held

Colombian security forces have stormed a supermarket in…

blocks.text: Colombian security forces have stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena, ending a daylong hostage siege, with the president saying all those held had been rescued and one hostage-taker killed.
Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 people were believed to be being held by armed men.
President Abelardo de la Espriella, said: “In an extraordinary joint operation between the national police and the armed forces, all the hostages were rescued.”

Shortly after midnight on Wednesday, a police helicopter was hovering low over the shopping centre as security forces massed outside the supermarket. Explosions then echoed around the complex as tactical teams moved in.
Ten of an estimated 30 people that were initially held had already been released during the 17-hour standoff, including several elderly women.
Moments later, soldiers could be seen inside the Éxito supermarket as security forces secured the building.

De la Espriella, who appeared at the scene wearing fatigues and carrying a sidearm and a walkie-talkie, described the operation as a success. He said: “We gave them the opportunity to surrender and free the hostages. They rejected that opportunity and we acted decisively.”
Cartagena’s mayor said all the hostages were “safe and sound” and would be reunited with their families before undergoing medical checks.
The siege gripped Cartagena, a Caribbean port famed for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship tourism. Supermarket employees had been among those feared trapped inside.

blocks.caption: Hostages inside the supermarket. Photograph: Sergio Jimenez Ciro/EPA

blocks.text: “My son is there,” Jacob Pérez, the father of one of the workers, said earlier in the standoff. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him.”
Images broadcast by Colombian media and shared online appeared to show masked gunmen in tactical gear alongside zip-tied hostages inside the store.

De la Espriella was quick to rule out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups. “It’s not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping – no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people,” he said.
Authorities said the siege began after an attempted robbery on an armoured vehicle at the shopping centre.

According to local media, the hostage-takers were demanding nearly US$2m (£1.5m), two armoured vehicles and safe passage to the city of Barranquilla, about 80 miles (130km) north-east of Cartagena. AFP could not independently verify those reports.

The siege began on the 10th anniversary of Colombia’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas amid a series of attacks across the country. Despite the deal to end the region’s largest insurgency, dissident guerrilla groups and criminal organisations still fight for control of parts of the country.
On Monday, authorities blamed a dissident Farc faction for a car bomb attack in the city of Villavicencio that wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.

Separately, the presidency said a “terrorist attack” on electrical infrastructure had disrupted power supplies in several south-western departments and prompted additional measures to protect energy facilities.
